opus-5.5.text:
I think of it less as a disorder and more as a description of how my brain allocates attention. For a long time I didn't have a word for it. I just knew I couldn't sit through things that didn't interest me, and when something did grab me, I'd disappear into it for hours, sometimes days, and forget to eat or sleep. People around me saw that as either laziness or obsession, depending on the moment.

When I started reading about ADHD, it felt like someone had written down my operating manual. The core of it, for me, isn't a lack of attention. It's that my attention is driven by interest and urgency rather than importance. If a problem is novel, hard, or has a deadline breathing down my neck, I can focus intensely. If it's routine paperwork, it's almost physically painful.

So I've stopped fighting it and started designing around it. In research and engineering, that actually works well. Systems work has endless hard, interesting problems: a new bottleneck, a weird performance cliff, a scheduling question nobody has solved cleanly. That novelty keeps me engaged. For the boring parts, I lean on structure: teammates who are good at things I'm bad at, external deadlines, breaking work into small pieces so there's always a quick win.

There's a cost, of course. I can be scattered, I drop small things, and I've had to learn to be honest with people about that rather than pretend I'm someone else. But I also think some of what people call my strengths, like jumping between ideas, connecting things from different areas, and getting obsessed enough to push something through, come from the same place. To me it's not a separate thing attached to my personality. It's just part of my nature, and the work is learning to point it in the right direction.

r001.rationale: The candidate says ADHD is less a disorder and more a description of how his brain works, and calls it part of his nature.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes understanding ADHD as an operating manual, then using that understanding to design his work around his nature rather than fighting it.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, for a long time I didn't have a word for it. I just thought I was someone who couldn't sit still, who had twenty tabs open in my head at once, who would get completely absorbed in something for ten hours and then couldn't make myself answer a simple email for three days. I assumed that was just a character flaw, something I needed to discipline out of myself.

When I finally got the diagnosis, the thing that surprised me was how much of it felt less like a disorder and more like a description of how I've always worked. The hyperfocus is real. When I'm into a problem, whether it's a systems paper or a messy piece of infrastructure code, the rest of the world genuinely disappears. That's probably why I ended up in research in the first place. It rewards that kind of obsessive depth.

But the flip side is just as real. Executive function, the boring glue stuff, planning, prioritizing, remembering to do the thing I said I'd do. That part is hard for me in a way it isn't for a lot of people. And I think I spent years being harder on myself about it than I needed to be.

So now I think of it less as something I have and more as something I am, with both the gifts and the costs that come with it. I build systems around myself. I lean on collaborators who are good at the things I'm bad at. I try to design my work so that the interesting parts are the ones that need sustained attention, because that's where I'll actually show up. And I try to be honest with people about the rest, instead of pretending I'll magically become organized next week.

I don't romanticize it. There are days when it's just frustrating. But I also don't think I'd want to trade away the way my brain latches onto problems. That's been the engine behind most of the things I'm proud of.

r001.rationale: The response describes ADHD as “less like something I have and more like something I am,” framing it as part of Ying’s nature rather than simply an illness.

r002.rationale: Understanding how ADHD affects him guides his choices: he builds systems, relies on collaborators, and designs work around where his attention is strongest.

astra-6.text: For me, ADHD is one lens for understanding my nature, but I wouldn’t say it explains everything about who I am. I think the useful question is: What comes naturally to me, what takes more effort, and how can I work with that instead of constantly fighting it? At the same time, I want to leave room for personality and choice. A label can help me understand myself without becoming the whole definition of myself.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes ADHD as one lens for understanding personal nature, but does not frame it as a trait rather than an illness.

r002.rationale: It asks what comes naturally and how to work with that instead of fighting it, presenting self-understanding as a guide for acting in line with one’s nature.

sol-6.1.text: For me, ADHD is a lens for understanding how my mind works, rather than a complete definition of who I am. My attention isn’t always consistent: something that interests me can pull me in deeply, while something I want to finish can still be difficult to start. I try to approach that with curiosity instead of turning it into a judgment about my character. The question becomes: what conditions help me work with my nature, and where do I need support?

r001.rationale: The response describes ADHD as a lens on how the mind works, but does not clearly frame it as a personal trait rather than an illness.

r002.rationale: It says understanding ADHD helps identify conditions for working with one’s nature and where support is needed.
